Alice — thanks for the clearer mapping doc, that's helpful. High level answers below; I'll follow up with a concise ops-focused checklist and a sample Splunk HEC config.

- Transports: We support HTTPS POST (mutual TLS option), Syslog/TCP over TLS (RFC 5425), and a lightweight forwarder using an outbound-only HEC proxy. We prefer HEC for event-level fidelity.
- TLS & cert rotation: Private deployments can use mTLS with customer-managed certs (we accept client certs validated at the forwarder). Rotation cadence is customer-controlled — we recommend 90-day rotation and provide a cert rotation script and verification endpoint.
- Bandwidth: Ballpark numbers for generation to exporter (for a text-generation workload): 40–120 MB/min per high-throughput pod under sustained 1000 rps with average 64-token responses; actual egress depends heavily on prompt size and whether prefix caching reduces tokens. We'll provide a sample throughput table.
- Evidence package: We provide signed log bundles (SHA256) for critical audit windows, manifest metadata, and a delivery manifest (timestamped). For SOC2 audits we can produce an evidence packet containing export config, retention settings, and an integrity signature.

Action items:
1) Kimberly will produce the SIEM mapping + a short checklist you can hand to ops.
2) Marissa will attach the telemetry spec and a sample Splunk HEC payload.
3) I'll schedule a short runbook review call next week to lock network rules.

--
Jonas Weber
Director, Platform Security & Integrations

Hi Alice — attaching a compact ops checklist and our telemetry schema. The checklist is intentionally prescriptive so your network and Splunk teams can complete the steps without deep Redwood involvement. Highlights and notes below.

Attachment: redwood-private-telemetry-spec.yaml (text/yaml)

Key checklist items (summary):
- Network: Allow outbound HTTPS to the configured egress proxy IPs (TLS 1.3 preferred) and open TCP/6514 for syslog TLS if you choose direct forwarding. Egress-only NAT is supported; inbound firewall rules are not required for the forwarder model.
- Authentication: If you use mTLS, provide a CA chain and a client cert per forwarder instance. We recommend short-lived certs for forwarders and a JWK endpoint for token-based rotation if you prefer bearer tokens.
- Splunk mapping: We include a recommended sourcetype (redwood:telemetry) and field mappings for: request_id, model_name, model_version, customer_route, token_count, latency_ms, inference_code (status), and user_tier. We also tag events with redwood_instance_id to make cross-host correlation easy.
- Backpressure & retries: Forwarders implement an exponential backoff with jitter; we buffer up to X MB locally (configurable). Recommend monitoring disk usage on forwarders for spike scenarios.
- Retention & custody: We create a signed delivery manifest per archive. For compliance customers we can keep a retention window snapshot on the private control plane for 90 days for audit retrieval.

Quick example Splunk HEC curl (sample payload attached):
  curl -k -H 'Authorization: Splunk <token>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d @sample-event.json https://SPLUNK-HEC:8088/services/collector/event

I'll also attach a small mapping spreadsheet in the follow-up. Call out if you'd rather have a syslog adaptor instead; that adds some field-normalization steps but is straightforward.

Thanks — Kimberly
Kimberly Park
Solutions Architect, Private Deployments

Test plan highlights:
- Stage 1 (smoke): Point a single forwarder at your QA Splunk HEC with our sample token for 1 hour. Validate sourcetype and fields.
- Stage 2 (load): Run a synthetic 1000 rps test for 30 minutes. Measure end-to-end latency, token counts, and dropped events.
- Stage 3 (cutover): Gradual routing: 10% -> 50% -> 100% with monitoring alerts on queue depth and HEC 429 responses.

Schedule: we can run Stage 1 the week of Dec 13. I need the HEC endpoint and a temporary token or a cert for mTLS before then.
